SANDF IN THE DRC

VO - The road to Phalaborwa in Limpopo…
It’s a world away from the violence and chaos of war-torn Democratic Republic of Congo, but the two places are now tragically entwined. It’s home to the Malesas, a family now in mourning.
Link - One of the soldiers that was killed in Goma is Corporal Matume "Justice" Malessa. And we've come to Palaborwa, where he's from, to speak to his family, find out how they're doing.
VO - Here, the community has gathered to share in their grief – one of 14 families saying their final farewells to loved ones… all of them soldiers killed in a firefight with rebels, in the eastern DRC cities of Goma and Sake late last month.
Govan: Do you know who killed Matume?
Mpho Monyela: No, we don't know who killed Matume. We don't know what killed Matume. We just received a message that they've been attacked. And Matume is no more.
Govan: Do you have any anger?
Mpho Monyela: No, I can't say it's an anger. I've been disappointed by the army management. If you don't equip your soldiers with enough equipment or reasonable resources to protect themselves, what else do you think they will get the resources to protect themselves?
VO – Matume had three children. His family tells me he was hoping to come home for his birthday.
VO - But everything changed when a rebel group called M23 – reportedly backed by the DRC’s neighbour, Rwanda – launched assaults on Goma and Sake.
VO – We have bases in both areas, as part of United Nations and Southern African Development Community missions. Debate is now raging around whether our soldiers were there as peacekeepers or a fighting force, and if they had enough weaponry and other support, to do either job properly.
Pikkie Greef: It's one of the most precarious situations that our military, in its entire history, has ever found itself in. If you're outgunned and you're outnumbered, then you can be the best soldiers in the world if you're going to lose the fight somewhere down the line.
VO - Pikkie Greef is from the SA National Defence Union. He’s long warned of how defence spending cuts are endangering the lives of SANDF soldiers deployed to places like the DRC.
Pikkie: Over the last decade, this SANDF budget has been slashed. Our spending on defense at 51 billion is about 0.7% of GDP, whereas the international norm is 2%. You know, cutting the defense budget over the past 15 years has done us no favors.
VO – And underspending by more than a percent of GDP can have dire consequences for a military committed to combat in foreign countries.
Govan: What did your members say about the attack and whether they could defend themselves?
Pikkie: If they had the necessary air support, at least then one could say they would have had a chance, or they wouldn't have ended up in the situation that they're in now.


VO – That “situation” remains perilous: Apart from the shocking casualties, our soldiers are now confined to base – at the mercy of M23.
Ironically, South Africa has homegrown attack helicopters called Rooivalk. In previous deployments in the DRC they developed a deadly reputation, providing crucial air support for our troops. This time round, the job was left to the DRC’s military, a notoriously ill-disciplined and poorly trained force.
Link: The conflict in the eastern DRC that's left a number of South African soldiers dead is complex and started a long time ago. …
VO: It’s impossible to separate the current turmoil in the DRC from a human calamity in neighbouring Rwanda three decades ago.
Rwandan society is divided into Hutu and Tutsi. In 1994, decades of resentment between the two, exploded into the mass slaughter of mainly Tutsis, by militia groups and the Hutu-dominated military.
Audio interlude
In the aftermath, some two million Hutus – many of whom had taken part in the killing – fled into eastern DRC where they remain to this day. Years of conflict and war have followed in which as many as six million people have died.
It’s in this turmoil that M23 has taken root, in support – they say – of the Congo’s Tutsi population, and where our soldiers have operated in various capacities since 1999.
Govan: What have you got over here?
Ricardo Texeira: That's M23 positions on the day. So already, by the time the battle began, the troops were almost entirely encircled, which forced troops to withdraw to Goma.
VO – Ricardo Texeira is a writer and analyst for the military publication Defence Web. He closely followed last month’s battle for Goma.
Ricardo: And M23 was then allowed to come around again and completely encircle the city.
Govan: And on this map, can you show me where the other South African troops were captured?
Ricardo: So at the airport in Goma, which is down here, this airstrip, that is where most of the troops were and where some of the troops are being held now.
Govan: Oh, so they're being held this close to the Rwandan border.
Ricardo: Yes, the runway is within mortar range of Rwanda. It's very close. It's right on the border.
VO: Rwanda’s proximity shows that it has legitimate security concerns: it’s denied backing M23, but the evidence is hard to ignore.
Ricardo: The UN has said that they've observed Rwanda troops crossing the border and joining M23, a Rwandan surface to air missile system fired on a UN drone. And a lot of the M23 fighters we have seen are wearing Rwa ndan-issued body armour. They are using Rwandan-issued weapons.
VO: But, as solid as the evidence against Rwanda appears..., critics make a similar claim against the SANDF.
Ricardo: the government keeps referring to it as peacekeeping, but it is not a peacekeeping operation. Those troops did not wear blue helmets. They are there under a peace enforcement mandate to assist the DRC in neutralizing armed rebel groups. So in essence, that involves a level of combat operations.
Govan: But the SADC troops' loyalty is to the DRC government, right?
Ricardo: Yes, in essence, we are an extension of their armed forces and operating under their direction and under a defensive mandate to assist them. We are party to the conflict.
VO – Our government disagrees, but Rwanda’s president – who once led the army that toppled Rwanda’s government and ended the 1994 genocide – had stern words for his counterpart.
Paul Kagame: I spoke with the president of South Africa. He's also there pretending to be playing a peacemaker role. And South Africa dares even issue threats. Of course, we will see what threats they are talking about.
VO – Fighting talk from a fighting head-of-state. While a war with Rwanda is highly unlikely, it’s none-the-less raised questions, over how the SANDF would fare in a full blown conflict.
Pikkie: If we were properly supported and equipped and properly funded, and this defense force was firing on all its cylinders, we wouldn't have to be negotiating for our soldiers' lives.
Govan: What are you saying? You don't think that we're ready for war?
Pikkie: No.
Govan: You don't?
Pikkie: We're not.


V/O – Late on Friday, unconfirmed reports emerged that the remaining SANDF soldiers in the DRC would be allowed to leave, but they’d need to leave their arms and equipment behind. An embarrassing outcome for our military.

Matume Malessa’s family, meanwhile, is searching for answers which – given the chaos of the DRC deployment - may never come.
Closing UPS
Mpho Monyela:
Watching his kids... they are still very young. Their father left home healthy, happy, smiling, knowing that he's going to work for his kids. But, only to find that he's not coming back. So, there's no way that we can be okay.

[END]



























PROMO 1


Outnumbered, out-gunned, and out-maneuvered…
Pikkie Greef: It's one of the most precarious situations that our military, in its entire history, has ever found itself in.
South African Soldiers trapped in the DRC, 14 confirmed dead.
Mpho Monyela: We just received a message that they've been attacked. And Matume is no more.

PROMO 2
A peace-keeping operation, or active combat?
Pikkie: The mission is to bring peace to the Eastern DRC. To have those parties who are causing the conflicts, either eliminated or to bring them to the negotiating table.
But are South African troops being hung out to dry?
Pikkie: SA Soldiers are very well trained and they’re tough. But you know, you can only do so much without proper support.

PROMO 3
A family in mourning, with very few answers…
Mpho Monyela: We don't know who killed Matume. We don't know what killed Matume.
Could events have played out differently during last month’s DRC conflict?
Pikkie: If we were properly supported and equipped and properly funded, and this defense force was firing on all its cylinders, we wouldn't have to be negotiating for our soldiers' lives.
